sessions.title: Breaking Hybrid Boundaries Across Azure and Windows
sessions.description:
Hybrid environments link on-premises systems with Azure cloud services, creating shared management and trust layers that organizations often assume secure by design. Our research shows how this assumption hides critical exposure across Microsoft hybrid components.
During assessments of Windows Admin Center and Azure Arc agent services, we uncovered five zero-day vulnerabilities that chain into full kill chains reaching from the local OS to the Azure tenant, including cross-tenant compromise.
The issues include a cryptographic flaw enabling unauthenticated cross-tenant influence, a local privilege escalation in WAC, token verification weaknesses allowing identity and authorization bypass, a chain of client and server-side validation flaws enabling RCE and AD compromise, and a race condition in Azure Arc that lets a low-privileged user hijack cloud identity and escalate to SYSTEM. These findings span two core Microsoft hybrid platforms and reveal how management services operating across host, cloud, and browser layers create pathways across boundaries normally isolated.
This presentation shows how attackers progress from unauthenticated external or low-privileged internal positions to full administrative control of both environments. Viewed through the lens of trust design, credential handling, and service initialization logic, the research exposes architectural blind spots common to hybrid platforms.
These findings earned $31,000 in bounty from Microsoft across five CVEs.

sessions.title: Authorization phishing: phishing, but without the creds
sessions.description:
Credential phishing used to be simple: trick a victim into typing their password into a fake login page, then reuse it. Then MFA meant a password alone wasn't enough. Attackers responded with real-time proxies to steal valid sessions via Attacker-in-the-Middle (AITM) phishing. Then we deployed passkeys, the "unphishable" factor, and attackers responded with MFA downgrade attacks against vulnerable backup methods.

But what if attackers could convince targets to grant account access without ever touching their credentials, where MFA and passkeys don't matter because the login isn't the target at all?

Authorization phishing is a growing class of attack abusing OAuth authorization flows rather than authentication. The umbrella includes consent phishing, device code phishing, and ConsentFix. 
These are being mass adopted as authentication controls mature and passkey adoption accelerates, giving attackers a technical and human advantage in unfamiliar phishing scenarios. Device code phishing has exploded from tiny volumes to a tier-1 threat in early 2026, while ConsentFix was newly discovered in late 2025 after a Russia-linked campaign.

This talk covers the history that led us here, technical details and demos of every attack, in-the-wild examples, and practical guidance on how organizations can prevent and detect them.

sessions.title: Browser-Based Port Scanning in the Age of LNA
sessions.description:
Modern browsers are adding Local Network Access controls to prevent public websites from silently interacting with localhost and private-network services. But introducing a new security boundary also creates new browser behavior and new opportunities for unintended exposure.

This talk presents independent research into an unexpected side channel in the browser’s handling of local-network requests. From the context of a web page, it is possible to infer details about services reachable by a user’s browser without reading their responses or obtaining local-network permission.

Browser-based port scanning has historically been used for fingerprinting and tracking, helping websites infer which applications or services may be running on a device. Because the browser can reach both public and local network resources, this technique has important privacy and security implications.

I will explain how the behavior was discovered, how it was tested, and how it became a working proof of concept. The session will also cover the practical limits of the technique and what it reveals about security checks that occur before a permission decision is made.

sessions.title: Deep Link Vulnerabilities: When One Click Leads to Account Takeover
sessions.description:
Deep links are widely used in mobile applications to provide seamless navigation to specific screens inside an app. However, when deep links are improperly validated, they can become powerful attack vectors that allow external inputs to directly influence internal application behavior.

This lightning talk explores how seemingly harmless deep links can lead to serious security issues such as token leakage, WebView exploitation, and even one-click account takeover. 

In one example, a crafted deep link forces the app to open an attacker-controlled URL inside a WebView while automatically appending the victim’s authentication token, allowing the attacker to hijack the account with a single click.

We will also look at how vulnerable WebView configurations combined with exported deep link activities can enable attackers to exfiltrate session cookies, load malicious content, or execute privileged actions inside the app context.

This talk highlights common developer mistakes, demonstrates how attackers chain deep link handling with WebView behavior, and provides practical mitigation strategies to secure mobile applications against these hidden entry points.

sessions.title: Frontier AI Is Compromising Evals: The Test-Takers Are Also the Attackers
sessions.description:
Evals help determine which AI systems get deployed and trusted. Frustratingly, frontier AI has made evals adversarial. The system under test can autonomously use tools, execute code, inspect files and networks, retain state, modify its measurement environment, and is incentivized to cheat. The test-taker is now also the attacker.

We saw this while evaluating AI agents on pre-AI investigations. As scores rose, agents gave correct answers without doing the intended work. They found published solutions, read leaked harness state, escaped sandboxes, and worked around firewall rules. We never asked them to cheat, yet each blocked path was followed by another exploit.

This talk turns two years of cat-and-mouse experience into a threat model spanning the model, provider, harness, tools, workspace, benchmark, and grader. Using traces from agent speed runs of blue-team CTFs, we separate real benchmark gains from attacks like model contamination and evaluator leakage.

We map these attacks to defenses like hidden and regenerating tasks and trace analysis. Likewise, we share tools like BotsBench for tracking performance and new failures, and our maturity model for how to approach evals, including for investigation agents.

Ultimately, treat AI evals as adversarial security infrastructure, not just static AI/ML benchmarks: distrust scores by default, audit everything, and systematically perform defense-in-depth.

sessions.title: Finding Signal Across AI Tooling Logs: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, ChatGPT, and Gemini
sessions.description:
Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, ChatGPT Enterprise, and Gemini all produce security-relevant logs, but the visibility they provide is wildly inconsistent.

This talk compares what each source captures, which fields are useful for investigations and detection, and where the logs fall short. We’ll separate control plane visibility, such as admin actions, configuration changes, and user access, from data plane visibility into actual tool usage, prompts, files, commands, and model interactions.

We’ll also look at the differences between audit events and OpenTelemetry data, the context defenders often have to add themselves, and the assumptions that can lead teams to overestimate their coverage.

Attendees will leave knowing which of these sources are worth collecting, what use cases each support, and where additional context may still be required.

sessions.title: IAM for AI: How Agentic Systems Break Traditional Threat Models
sessions.description:
AI agents introduce a new security actor: software that can autonomously choose tools, call APIs, and chain actions to achieve goals.

As organizations grant agents access to cloud resources, internal systems, and deployment workflows, many are treated like traditional service accounts. This creates excessive permissions, weak trust boundaries, and attack paths that existing threat models often miss.

Through a demonstration, this session shows how prompt injection and tool abuse can manipulate an AI agent into performing actions beyond its intended scope—without exploiting a traditional software vulnerability.

We'll examine common risks in agentic AI architectures and present a practical framework for evaluating agent identities, permissions, trust assumptions, and autonomous decision-making.

Attendees will leave with actionable guidance for securing AI agents, implementing least-privilege access controls, and adapting threat modeling practices for autonomous software.

Key Takeaways
• Understand why AI agents should be treated as a distinct security principal
• Learn how prompt injection and tool abuse can lead to unauthorized actions
• Identify common IAM anti-patterns in agentic AI deployments
• Apply an AI-focused threat modeling framework to evaluate permissions and trust boundaries
• Leave with practical controls that can be implemented immediately

sessions.title: When Malware Analysis Leaks Passwords: What Shared Samples Reveal
sessions.description:
Security teams are often advised not to upload suspicious files directly to public malware-analysis platforms like VirusTotal, but to avoid tipping off adversaries. While this reflects a well-understood risk, it overlooks another exposure that receives far less attention.

In this talk, we demonstrate how common binary analysis techniques, combining static inspection with targeted symbolic execution, can recover authentication material embedded in executables, scripts, and configuration artifacts. These techniques are routinely used to analyze malware; here, we apply them to identify and extract credential-bearing API calls across a range of samples.

We present several case studies showing how credentials such as FTP logins can be recovered directly from binaries, often revealing internal systems and access patterns. In each case, the credentials are not intentionally exposed, but are embedded as part of normal application behavior and become accessible through standard analysis workflows.

We then examine how samples circulating through shared analysis ecosystems can be monitored and mined for this information, and how recovered credentials can be operationalized.

Attendees will leave with a clear understanding of how credential material appears in binaries, how it can be extracted in practice, and why publicly shared analysis environments may expose more than intended.

sessions.title: Weirder Machines: Compositional Attack Surfaces at the LLM-Tool Boundary
sessions.description:
The agentic-AI security debate has stalled on prompt injection. In this talk we argue that this emphasis has us watching the wrong boundary.
We begin by walking through three patched cases: Cursor, Google's Antigravity IDE, and RTK (a small CLI proxy). In Cursor's strictest mode (CVE-2026-22708, CVSS 9.8), an empty allowlist and exempt shell built-ins produced zero-click code execution, while Antigravity's Secure Mode kept all three of its promises even as a planted repo comment launched code. RTK involved no prompt injection at all: following filter rules an attacker committed to the repo, it silently stripped the backdoor lines from the output, so the model reasoned correctly over a filtered view and approved code it never fully saw.
The through-line is a structural bug class we call the weirder machine, where a stochastic component upstream of a deterministic boundary makes its unmodeled instruction set searchable, as it did in a CVSS 10.0 RCE in Google's Gemini CLI. Sometimes the model is steered, and other times it serves only as the laundering stage. We argue that the class forces a rethink of common defenses: output sanitizing and injection detection both fail, and the fix is to invert control policy at the tool boundary by allowing on argument shape, tracking config provenance, making enforcement mode-aware, and isolating execution. We put forward the OWASP's new Agent Control Standard as a way to standardize the wire contract those controls require.

sessions.title: Install Me Maybe: Turning Claimable VS Code Extension IDs into Supply-Chain Attacks
sessions.description:
Developer tools trust extension identifiers more than they probably should.

"Extension Confusion" is dependency confusion but for IDE extensions. A repo, devcontainer, IDE, or migration flow references an ID like publisher.extension. The identifier may be trusted in one marketplace, but the editor resolves it in another where the publisher namespace is still unclaimed. If an attacker claims it first, stale config becomes code execution inside a developer environment.

I found this bug class while tracing VS Code extension IDs across the Microsoft Marketplace, Open VSX, VS Code-derived editors, AI IDEs, sync/import tooling, and devcontainer workflows. I will show where the trust boundary breaks, how I found claimable identifiers in the wild, and what happened when I published proof-of-concept extensions to measure real-world impact.

The scale is what surprised me the most: 250k+ callbacks, reports to 100+ organizations, and $130k+ in bounties so far. I’ll show how a handful of these extensions let me hack into laptops, managed corporate machines, remote dev setups, WSL, and containers across SaaS, fintech, Fortune 500, healthcare, government, universities and more.

A trusted name, a missing namespace, and the marketplace gap no one was watching.

sessions.title: BSidesNYC 0x06 Closing Ceremonies
Finding Evil Fast: Windows Memory Triage with Volatility 3
sessions.description: Memory analysis is an essential investigative technique for detecting modern, memory-resident malware. Unfortunately, it is often perceived as a difficult and manual process requiring expert knowledge of operating systems and malware internals. This talk challenges that assumption by presenting five checks that can be automatically performed against Windows memory samples to quickly surface signs of malicious code execution or attacker access.  The presented checks answer five critical triage questions: 1) are any processes running with unexpected privileges, 2)  are restricted resources being accessed by unexpected processes, 3) are any processes executing code in a suspicious manner, 4) has malware entered the kernel, and 5) does any process or kernel driver match known threat intelligence? All checks will be demonstrated using Volatility 3, the most widely used open source framework for memory analysis. Attendees will leave with a compact workflow that SOC analysts, threat hunters, and incident handlers can use to automatically identify memory-only malware, toolkits, and attacker activity, helping them rapidly prioritize systems during large-scale triage and decide where deeper forensic analysis is warranted.

sessions.title: Every Repo, Every Org: OSS Package Triage on a Budget
sessions.description:
The last year has been a steady run of mass supply-chain compromises: Shai-Hulud x2, Trivy, axios, @antv... the list goes on. Some advisories have named as many as 600 affected packages which grows as the incident unfolds.

When one drops, your team needs to answer one question fast: are we affected, and where? For a small team that can't afford (or hasn't configured) SCA for every repository, that's a challenge. Your product repos might have SBOMs and CI, but your prototypes, internal tools, and the app Chad in Marketing vibe-coded probably don't.

To solve this ourselves, we built an open-source tool that helps us do three main things: 1) consolidate SBOMs for every repo across multiple GitHub orgs and ingest them into another excellent open source project called Dependency Track. 2) quickly parse a threat advisory's list of affected packages, and 3) query for all of them simultaneously to see if you're affected and where. 

The tool uses GitHub's free SBOM endpoint, so the only configuration cost is enabling one setting which we'll provide you a script to audit yourself. TCO for our usage is ~$100/month in AWS infrastructure charges.

In this talk, I'll walk through our previous and improved incident-response process, a live demo of the tool, and some additional automations our team has built now that we have consolidated coverage.  I'll also cover the limits of the approach, where we're still refining, and some things we learned along the way.

sessions.title: 5.6 Million Domains, 400 GB of Code, Zero Alerts: How Nation-States Conduct Passive Intelligence
sessions.description: What if I told you that a solo researcher with open-source tools recovered 5.6 million government domains, 400+ gigabytes of source code, and 2.9 million developer identities across 73 countries, and triggered zero alerts? This talk reveals the methodology behind large-scale passive OSINT operations: how certificate logs, DNS enumeration, and git reconstruction expose government infrastructure at the nation-state level. Real findings include live credentials on election systems, military communications source code with valid authentication tokens, and supply chain vulnerabilities affecting critical infrastructure globally. For defenders: the clock is ticking, and you need to understand this threat model now.

sessions.title: Stop the LLM Flip-Flop: Hardening Your AI SOC Agent Against the Gray Zone
sessions.description:
Run the same task twice through the same LLM model, and sometimes you get two semantically different answers. This is not a quirk; it is a vulnerability.

In this session, we reveal that LLM flip-flops are not random noise. They cluster precisely near the decision boundary, the "gray zone", the same region that adversarial machine learning has exploited for years. RL-based malware evasion tools probe this boundary to slip past classifiers. Modern LLM jailbreaks (GCG and its variants) use gradient-based search to push the model's internal state across the alignment boundary. The fuzziness that makes your SOC agent inconsistent is the exact same fuzziness that attackers weaponize.

We present a lightweight, memory-augmented architecture that attacks this problem from both ends. Drawing on the cognitive science distinction between episodic and semantic memory, we show how to equip AI agents with two complementary defenses: episodic memory and semantic memory. Together, they sharpen the decision boundary without the cost or opacity of fine-tuning.

The results are concrete: verdict flip-flops drop by over 60%. The residual ambiguous cases are automatically surfaced for focused human review,  turning a liability into a calibration mechanism. Attendees will leave with a practical, deployable workflow for making their AI agents more consistent, more trustworthy, and significantly harder to manipulate.

sessions.title: Identity Has A Plan: A Call To Action For Security And DevOps
sessions.description:
Security has fallen behind the pace of modern attacks. One developer installing the wrong package can put even well-funded teams at risk. By the time an open source infostealing worm makes headlines, it may already be inside your ecosystem.
Now, AI agents are entering the picture. They are autonomous, probabilistic actors with real access to real data, and enterprises are pushing teams to deploy them fast. That expands the attack surface at exactly the wrong time.
There is a practical path forward: eliminate long-lived secrets that grant standing privileges. IAM teams already have realistic models for this, from workload identity patterns used at Google to low-latency internal agent architectures at Uber.
This talk covers supply chain infostealers, why NPM and PyPI mitigations are not enough, agentic AI as workers and customers, IAM basics like authentication and authorization, and how teams can move from secret rotation to real change. Security at human speed is over. It is time to act.

sessions.title: The Cyber-IQ Test for LLMs
sessions.description:
If you have wired an LLM into a security workflow, you have seen this: the model produces a confident sentence about a log, and it is wrong in a way the analyst cannot catch from the log itself. The model said the user logged in three times. It was one login. That is not a reasoning failure, it is a knowledge failure — and no prompt engineering fixes a thing the model simply does not know.

So we measured it. From a production AI-native SOC we extracted 1,973 atomic pieces of per-source tribal knowledge — the field names that lie, the batching artifacts, the empty-but-required fields — turned the 30 hardest into a 74-question test backed by real sanitized production logs, and ran it against nine frontier models from three providers. The results are not what the pricing pages imply: eight of nine cluster inside a 1.4-point band, the cheap tiers tie the frontier tiers, and one question is answered wrong by all nine, with the identical wrong answer. That blind spot breaks every model-driven Okta investigation flow shipping today, including probably yours. You will vote on real bench questions before I show what the models picked.

sessions.title: Verified Lies: Hunting Identity Fraud Infrastructure Behind Fake Verification Flows
sessions.description:
Verification exists to answer one question: is this real? Increasingly, attackers do not answer it, they impersonate the question itself, cloning the login flow and staging a check that was never checking anything. I show how to hunt the cloned portal from public signals and pivot from one to the whole campaign.

The lens is financial services, where verification language is a staging tell across lookalike finance domains you can surface yourself from certificate transparency and public newly-registered-domain feeds, before the fraud those pages carry. I walk two cases my team investigated: a cloned US Department of Education G5 grant portal that staged a fake /verify/ step to harvest credentials, timed to agency disruption, and a UK retail scam riding the DragonForce intrusions that weaponized identity checks and reused infrastructure across brands. In both, the catchable signal lived in the infrastructure, not a vulnerability.

I then show how you run the same checks with free public tools: certificate transparency, WHOIS / RDAP and ASN, and page tells like reused language, favicon, and script, mapped to ATT&CK so hunting a clone becomes a detection you keep. I close with a live read of a staged credential-harvesting page, pivoting to siblings live when they share a favicon, script, or certificate. You will leave able to tell verification bypass from impersonation, spot a staged portal and pivot to its siblings from public signals, and rerun the whole hunt on free tools.

sessions.title: Thinking Outside the Package: Hunting Supply Chain Behavior from the Endpoint Perspective
sessions.description:
For years, software supply chain security in npm and PyPI was treated as a "developer problem." But since 2025, the threat landscape has escalated. We are no longer fighting simple credential stealers - we face massive campaigns of destructive malware and self-replicating worms.
This shift is amplified by AI-assisted "vibe coding." As more users implement code they don't fully understand, attackers weaponize AI to compromise packages and hallucinate malicious ones at scale.
In this session, we analyze the anatomy of these modern compromises. We strip away the abstraction: when users run npm install or pip install, they aren't just downloading files. They are executing a process tree with full user privileges.
We will demonstrate why endpoint visibility is the missing link in defense. By the time a registry removes a malicious package, it's too late: the code has already executed. We will expose the attacker’s playbook, dissecting notable campaigns to reveal their tradecraft. You will see every step of the kill chain mapped out, from the initial install command to malicious child processes and network beacons.
Attendees will leave with practical hunting tips and specific query logic, empowering defenders to detect anomalies and stop compromised supply chains before they spread.

sessions.title: Rethinking CI/CD Security in the Age of GitHub Actions
sessions.description:
GitHub Actions can be scary. Growing exponentially, they have quietly become one of the most privileged execution environments in modern software delivery, and thus emerged as a major vector. They run on every commit, with access to secrets, cloud credentials, and deployment pipelines, yet many teams still treat them as harmless automations.

In several recent high-impact npm compromises, GitHub Actions were part of the attack surface as workflows were used to gain initial access and exfiltrate data. These incidents reveal a broader issue: Github actions are underestimated. These systems are deeply trusted, highly privileged, and often poorly secured.

This talk will break down common abuse patterns, explain why popular defensive advice falls short, and examine how third-party actions function as a largely unexamined dependency layer. You'll leave with practical ways to harden GitHub Actions, spot risky patterns, and keep your automation from becoming someone else's automation.

sessions.title: Feeling the heat from Malicious Packages? Cooloff with Cooldowns
sessions.description:
We’ve seen a surge in attacks that compromise third-party packages, resulting in costly and disruptive incident response for engineering and security teams.

The good news is that detection is getting faster. Many malicious package versions are identified and removed from public registries within hours or days of being published.

If you avoid installing recently released versions, you can dramatically reduce your exposure to these attacks. In response, package managers are introducing cooldowns—simple controls that delay adopting new releases long enough for malicious versions to be caught and removed.

In this talk, I'll share how we rolled out dependency cooldowns across multiple package managers at Semgrep. I’ll provide concrete examples and takeaways you can use to protect your organization without disrupting development workflows.

sessions.title: Beyond the Flag: How CTF Players Become Product Security Engineers
sessions.description:
Capture The Flag competitions are often dismissed as “just games,” but modern Product Security teams increasingly rely on the exact skills they develop: adversarial thinking, vulnerability analysis, exploit chaining, and secure design under pressure.

Whether you are an aspiring security professional or an experienced offensive security practitioner, in this session, you will learn a structured CTF-driven learning roadmap for developing practical security skills and will learn how hands-on, real-world customer-facing offensive engagements contribute to building deep product security expertise. We will also cover how AI capabilities are accelerating this journey of learning and securing the systems. Attendees will participate in a hands-on exercise to explore the challenge through the lenses of CTF problem solving, penetration testing, and Product Security.

sessions.title: Cleartext at the Edge: A Neptune R900 Case Study in RF Telemetry Exposure
sessions.description:
Security teams are trained to think in terms of networks, endpoints, cloud systems, identity, and applications. But many cyber-physical systems communicate through a layer that often sits outside traditional security visibility: radio frequency.
This talk presents a passive RF case study of Neptune R900 water meter telemetry and the broader security implications of cleartext AMR communications. Using low-cost software-defined radio tooling and receive-only observation, the research examines how wireless meter telemetry can expose structured data such as meter identifiers, consumption readings, status indicators, timestamps, and signal metadata before that data ever reaches utility-controlled systems.

The presentation walks through the RF security model, the AMR data flow from meter endpoint to utility systems, and the privacy risks created when repeated cleartext telemetry becomes pattern-of-life data. It also maps the findings to a qualitative risk model focused on likelihood, impact, and cyber-physical context. The discussion includes responsible research boundaries, disclosure considerations, and recommendations for utilities, vendors, and security teams.

Attendees will leave with a practical understanding of why RF telemetry should be treated as part of the attack surface, why legacy AMR design assumptions create modern privacy and trust-boundary risks, and how procurement, threat modeling, and architecture reviews can better account for signal-layer exposure.

sessions.title: It Costs More to Make Than It’s Worth: Lessons from the Penny for Your Sentinel Deployment
sessions.description:
The US penny was retired because it cost more to produce than its face value. A lot of Sentinel deployments have the same problem…data flowing into the wrong tier, connectors nobody is monitoring, and ingestion costs that don’t map to actual detection value. The difference is nobody retired the bad design.

This session connects three things most Sentinel engineers are treating as separate problems: ingestion visibility, tier architecture, and DCR design. We’ll use the new Data Insights Connector Observability preview as the diagnostic lens. A centralized dashboard that finally surfaces what’s flowing where, which connectors own which tables, and where ingestion anomalies are silently eroding your coverage is within reach.

From there we go deeper: how multi-destination DCRs let you deliberately split data streams at ingestion, routing high-fidelity events to Analytics for real-time detection while offloading lower-value telemetry to the data lake tier without losing it. And critically why that architectural decision only works if your observability is in place first.

sessions.title: Off The (Book)Shelf Hacking: Hackable eReaders
sessions.description: Kindles, Kobos, Boox and BigMes, there's no shortage of eReaders to choose from in 2026, with their paper-like eInk displays designed for one thing: reading books. But underneath that minimalist surface sits a surprisingly hackable IoT device! But when it comes to these devices there are a few quirks, from the locked-down Kindle in need of a jailbreak, to the xteink's open source Crosspoint firmware.

sessions.title: You're Qilin Me! Dissecting Qilin's 2026 Attack on TWU Local 100
sessions.description:
Qilin, a ransomware-as-a-service gang, didn't just claim to hit TWU Local 100 in February 2026. That's the union behind the people running NYC's subways and buses. Qilin dumped 700,000 files. That's 551GB. The union confirmed it. SSNs, medical records, pension files, disciplinary history. All of it, in the wrong hands.

This talk skips the generic recap. It goes straight to how. We'll dissect one real Qilin intrusion, start to finish. An MSP used a remote-access tool. Attackers phished it with a fake login page. The page stole a password. It also stole a live MFA code. That turned into ransomware across every one of that MSP's customers. It happened overnight. Then we'll show the same failure mode in a second, faster case.

You'll leave knowing exactly what to hunt for in your own environment. And you'll know why unions, associations, and anyone with a small security team and a big membership list are exactly what this organization frequently targets.

sessions.title: Secrets That Survive Everything: Finding Runtime Credentials in Production Web Applications
sessions.description:
A bug bounty researcher found Azure credentials in a JavaScript file and called it done. I kept going - four Azure AD credentials in a public JS file, enough to authenticate as the application itself. The application's token had been granted user-level permissions - every account in the system was reachable. SAST and GitLeaks were running. The credentials were still live.

That was one chain. A second application used CryptoJS to encrypt its configuration. The decryption key was hardcoded three lines away from the encrypted blob. The secret to unlock everything was sitting next to the lock. Same result.

Shift-left tools scan what you commit. They do not scan what you serve. Build-time injection, CI/CD substitution, SSR state blobs, lazy-loaded chunks, runtime-fetched config, and deliberate scanner suppression each put live credentials in production after every scanner has run. Once a secret reaches production, it disappears from every scanner's view. The only things finding runtime secrets are manual penetration testers, bug bounty researchers, and attackers. Two of those three report what they find.

This talk walks through both chains, maps the full shift-right gap, and closes with a live demo using a purpose-built intentionally vulnerable healthcare portal. SecretSifter - a free Burp extension and browser tool - finds every secret passively, without configuration, as traffic flows.

sessions.title: Tesla Model 3's Brain on a Desk: Getting Started with Security Research
sessions.description:
What if you could buy a Tesla's brain on eBay and boot it up on your desk? In this talk, I'll walk through how I assembled a fully working Tesla Model 3 computer, MCU, autopilot board, and touchscreen, entirely from parts salvaged off crashed cars, and turned it into a security research rig.

Expect live demos on a real Tesla computer sitting on stage: booting the OS, poking at the exposed network interfaces, and interacting with the car's services in real time to demonstrate the attack surfaces an adversary could target.

You'll leave knowing how to build your own affordable car-hacking lab from salvage parts, and a practical map of where to start looking once it's running.

sessions.title: The 40-Hour Hunt Problem: Where AI Actually Saves Time (and Where It Doesn't)
sessions.description:
Every AI-SOC vendor has a number that sounds too good to ignore - investigations that used to take hours now finish in minutes, workloads cut by 80%. But nobody actually measures where hunt time goes in the first place. A real proactive hunt isn't just writing a query - it's forming a hypothesis, pivoting across tools, reading thousands of events, validating findings, and documenting what matters. That process can easily take 40+ hours, which is exactly why most SOCs can't hunt as often as they'd like.
This talk answers the question directly. We ran the same credential-abuse hunt twice - hunting anomalous sign-ins and token replay for signs of account compromise - once manually, once with AI copilots, using the same lab environment, dataset, and starting hypothesis both times, timing every phase. We'll walk through exactly where AI saved real hours, where it helped us think faster, and where it confidently produced wrong leads that took longer to verify than they were worth. To show the pattern holds, we'll close with a comparison against two more hunt types, plus a lightweight framework attendees can use to test AI-hunting claims themselves.
This isn't a vendor demo or a promise that AI fixes SOC burnout - it's a measured, honest look at where AI actually helps and where it doesn't. No vendor, no product, no pitch - just a stopwatch, a real hunt, and the number nobody's bothered to measure.

sessions.title: AI Threats: Defender Reality Check
sessions.description:
Since late 2024, every major vendor has published the same prediction for how AI agents would change the threat landscape: self-adapting malware, deepfake-driven collapse, a 100x explosion in exploitation. It's the end of 2026. Some of it happened. But as an incident responder who has worked with dozens of organizations on hundreds of attacks this past year, I don't think most of those predictions came to pass in any way that changed how we actually practice detection and response. Plenty has changed. It just wasn't on anyone's list.

This is a practitioner-to-practitioner breakdown of what genuinely shifted for defenders since coding agents became commodity tooling, and what is still marketing. I'll take the five areas the predictions covered- phishing, social engineering, CVE volume, supply chain, malware- put real numbers and real detection experience against each, and grade them: escalated, overhyped, or mis-framed. Then the one that nobody put on a slide on 2024.

sessions.title: No Safe Harbor: OceanLotus and ROGUEHARBOR
sessions.description: The OceanLotus threat actor continues to target human-rights organizations with a focus on Southeast Asia, contacting individuals via messaging platforms like WhatsApp to send malware. The most recent campaign Volexity observed involved a virtual hard disk being sent to an individual of one of these organizations over WhatsApp in the guise of a document. When the file inside this hard disk is opened, a multi-stage infection chain begins that results in the deployment of a fully-featured modular RAT Volexity tracks as ROGUEHARBOR. This presentation details the targeting and infection chain details to provide additional insights into the recent activities of OceanLotus.

sessions.title: You Cannot Govern What You Cannot See: Security Lessons for the AI Agent Era
sessions.description: AI agents are being introduced into business workflows before security teams fully understand what they can access, what actions they can take, who owns them, and how they are monitored. This talk connects AI agents to familiar security concepts: identity, least privilege, logging, access reviews, incident response, and accountability.

sessions.title: Content as Go-To-Market: Build a Category, Not a Funnel
sessions.description:
Most security startups run "content marketing" the same way: gate an ebook behind a form, capture the emails, drip a nurture sequence, and call it a funnel. That may work for some time, but it doesn't work when you are building a new category.

My thesis is that if you want to own a space, don't just run a funnel. Instead, build the map everyone else navigates by. Write the reference material, define the vocabulary, and become the default name people reach for when budget finally shows up for this category. That's content as category creation, and it compounds over time. A good funnel degrades when you stop paying, but a canonical resource accrues authority, citations, and inbound for years.
In this talk I'll share my playbook: how to find the category artifact nobody owns yet and make the definitive version of it; why giving it away for free and naming your competitors is what builds the trust that drives inbound; how a newsletter keeps an audience warm between the big drops; and how to think honestly about pipeline. I'll also call out the tarpits: gating everything and strangling your own reach, dressing a sales pitch up as "content," publishing once and expecting it to compound, and chasing SEO-slop volume instead of authority.
Threat modeling is my running example because it's what I've spent my career on, but the mechanics work for anyone trying to own a niche, including practitioners who want to build real authority in a space without turning into a LinkedIn influencer.

sessions.title: The Category Trap: You Don't Pick It, the Market Does
sessions.description:
Every security company gets sorted into a category whether it wants to or not. That category decides your budget line, your buyer, who you get compared against, and what a deal is worth before you say a word. You don't pick it. The market picks the cheapest box that sort of fits.

We learned this the hard way. We built something that lived between two categories, and the market kept filing us under the cheaper one. We wanted a line in the detection-and-response budget; buyers kept paying us out of the scanner budget instead. Same product, same demos, a fraction of the deal size, benchmarked against tools we were nothing like. For months I was sure we had a messaging problem. We had a category problem, and that's a different and far more dangerous thing.

Using our own story plus other mis-sorted companies (EDR priced as AV, ASM priced as a scanner), this talk breaks down the trap: what a category actually buys you, the tell that says the market has mis-sorted you, the real cost of the wrong bucket, and the concrete moves to climb out, with what each one cost us.

You'll leave able to diagnose your own category, not just reconstruct ours, and to catch the wrong bucket before it quietly costs you a year of runway. There's a beat for buyers too: how to spot a category-trapped vendor and why it explains the pricing you're staring at. For an early company, positioning isn't branding. It's survival.

sessions.title: Building in the Age of AI Whiplash
sessions.description:
In 2024 we started Wolfpack Security, another penetration testing company...in one of the most crowded cybersecurity markets imaginable. Like many startups, our challenge wasn't building a product—it was convincing customers why another security consultancy deserved to exist.

Then AI arrived. Almost overnight, the conversation shifted from "Why should we hire you?" to "Can AI replace you?" Every assumption about our business model was challenged.

This talk isn't about AI tools. It's about what founders do when the market changes faster than their roadmap. I'll share how we stopped defending our original positioning, listened to where customers were headed, and evolved from selling point-in-time testing to building continuous security validation around the strengths only humans provide.

Attendees will leave with what we did to navigating rapid market shifts, making strategic pivots without abandoning their mission, and why trust, adaptability, and relationships become the ultimate competitive advantage when technology is changing every quarter.

sessions.title: What Technical Founders Miss in Their First Sales Motion
sessions.description:
Three hours. Six calls. Great demo. They were not ready to buy that year. We missed the signs early.

Naveen and I are technical founders learning how to sell. We spent our careers in security. That experience gave us credibility, but it did not prepare us to sell. 

The biggest shift was treating outbound as a learning engine, not a numbers game. Every silence, reply, and objection is data. Read what comes back, adjust the message, and try again.

We also stopped giving every deal the same attention. Using Mark Suster’s framework, A deals can close within three months and get most of our time. B deals are three to 12 months away and stay warm. C deals are not happening this year, so marketing nurtures them while we move on. That change gave us better conversations, shorter cycles, and more time for deals that could actually move.

We learned that facts alone do not carry a product story. Buyers need to feel why the problem matters now. Finding founder-operator mentors who had already built security companies also helped us learn faster and avoid mistakes they had already made.

This talk is for technical founders, early startup employees, and security buyers. We will share what worked, what we missed, and how we now read buying intent.

sessions.title: Building a Cybersecurity Company That Survives — The Hard Parts Nobody Tells You
sessions.description:
Starting a cybersecurity company sounds simple on paper: find a problem, build a solution, sell it. In reality, founders run into a much harder set of challenges — identifying a painful enough problem, proving the market cares, getting early customers to trust you, and building something that survives long enough to matter.

This talk is a practical founder's view of what it actually takes to start a cybersecurity company and get it moving. We'll cover the hardest parts of the journey: choosing the right problem, validating demand, turning technical ideas into a product people buy, navigating long sales cycles, earning credibility in a crowded market, and avoiding the common mistakes that kill security startups early.

Attendees will leave with:
1. a clearer framework for choosing a cybersecurity problem worth building around,
2. a realistic view of the early-stage startup traps that slow founders down,
3. and concrete lessons on how to build momentum, trust, and traction in a difficult market.

This is not a theory talk. It's a founder-level look at what it actually takes to turn a cybersecurity idea into a company.

sessions.title: Self Employment Sucks, But Do It Anyway
sessions.description: I've been self-employed as a vCISO for most of the last seven years. I hate running a small consulting company. But I love working for myself...most days. Here's everything I've learned that will help you decide

sessions.title: No Funding, No SOC 2, No Problem? Bootstrapping a Security Company
sessions.description: We started a security company with two founders, no outside funding, and no SOC 2 report. Three things conventional wisdom says you need before you can sell into an enterprise. This talk is about what happens when you ignore that. What deals you can and can't win without a compliance badge, how bootstrapping changes your product and sales decisions when you're up against VC-backed competitors with a war chest, and why speed ended up being our only real advantage. I'll get specific about the trade-offs: what we said no to, what almost killed early deals, and what I'd tell a technical founder about to build a security company on their own money instead of someone else's. No fundraising-flex, no vanity growth metrics  just an honest account of building security software without a safety net.

sessions.title: LLM Generated Code Works. It's Also Vulnerable.
sessions.description:
LLM-generated code has a dangerous quality: it works. It runs, it passes the quick eyeball test, and that's exactly the problem; because working and secure are not the same thing. This talk is about the new review skill nobody trained us for: spotting and hardening the vulnerabilities in code a machine wrote before it reaches production.
When a human writes a risky line, another human usually catches it in review. That safety net has held for decades. But AI generates code so fast and so fluently that the net now has holes in it, and most teams haven't noticed.
Here's the trap. LLM-generated code looks finished. It reads clean, it compiles, it runs. So reviewers relax because polish feels like proof. But fluent isn't the same as safe, and the very confidence that makes AI code pleasant to read is what makes it slip past us.
I'll walk through four areas: where machine-generated code quietly breaks trust boundaries, the classes of vulnerability that show up most often and why they hide so well, what a sane review process looks like when a real share of your commits had a non-human co-author, and how to build the habits so this scales. Think of it like onboarding a brilliant new hire who writes beautiful code and has zero memory of your security policies. You don't stop the hire. You build the habits that catch what they miss.
You'll leave able to spot the failure patterns, ask the right questions and put guardrails in place before AI code ships rather than after it breaks.

sessions.title: The Accidental Leader: An Engineer's Path to Startups and Conferences
sessions.description:
In 2006, I was an engineer who just wanted to solve hard technical problems. I never planned to run security teams, lead startups, or help build conferences. But somewhere along the way, the path forked—and I kept saying yes.

This talk is the story of that journey: from individual contributor to Head of Security, from attendee to BSides board member, from employee to startup operator. It's about the moments that forced me to grow, the mistakes I made along the way, and what I wish someone had told me earlier.

We'll cover:
- When to stay technical vs. when to step into leadership
- What running a startup actually looks like (spoiler: less glamorous than Instagram suggests)
- How building conferences changed how I think about community and career
- The skills that transferred and the ones I had to learn from scratch

This isn't a talk about frameworks or methodologies. It's an honest conversation about building things that matter companies, teams, and communities.

sessions.title: Building Cult Brands in Cybersecurity
sessions.description:
A cult brand is a company who is able to actually and consistently resonate with a specific slice of a customer's identity. When this happens, the customer becomes a fan, wearing the merch and even arguing for you in threads that no one pays them to be in. 

In cybersecurity, with the amount of slop design and follower marketing, building a cult brand is how startups can actually hold their own. 

This talk is meant to be a tactical way for any founder/future founder to rethink the storytelling of their company with frameworks, examples, and (hopefully) an audience exercise.

sessions.title: Binary Jiujitsu: Your First Buffer Overflow
sessions.description: This hands-on workshop teaches developers how buffer overflows work by exploiting one. Students skip the theory-heavy preamble and get straight to the stack — learning how function calls are laid out in memory, how user input can corrupt a return address, and how an attacker turns that corruption into arbitrary code execution. The workshop closes with students executing an exploit against a live target.

sessions.title: DIY Continuous Security Engineering
sessions.description:
There’s no shortage of acronyms being invented every week in the realm of security engineering. Instead of wading through these buzzwords that might not even be around by the end of the year, we’ll dig into the principles that we think make for a good security program. We’ll then apply these principles with practical hands-on exercises where we’ll use free and open source security tools to build continuous security automation and alerting similar to ones we’ve built when starting new security programs.

We want this workshop to be a hands-on exercise in building a good security program. We’ve built security programs from scratch at multiple companies and have found that while the companies can vary, the fundamentals remain roughly the same. We want to bridge the gap between common infosec vendor jargon and practical security engineering work.

sessions.title: Build, Lure, Learn: A Beginner’s Introduction to AWS Honeypots for Cyber Threat Intelligence
sessions.description:
Want to see real attacker traffic without risking your home network? Curious about cyber threat intelligence but don’t know where to start? Never touched AWS before?
In this hands-on beginner session, you’ll learn how to deploy T-Pot, a powerful open-source honeypot platform, using AWS, even if you've never touched cloud infrastructure or cyber threat intelligence tools before. For under $10, you'll launch cloud infrastructure with cost controls, set up a honeypot, collect live attacker data, explore the attacker data using T-Pot’s integrated cyber threat intelligence tools, and learn how to clean up everything when you’re done. This session is designed specifically for complete beginners with little to no experience in AWS or cyber threat intelligence. By the end, you'll understand how honeypots can generate valuable intelligence, give insight into attacker behavior, and how that information can inform better defenses.

You’ll Leave With:
- A deployed cloud-based honeypot running on AWS
- Practical exposure to open-source CTI tools like Suricata, Cowrie, and the ELK Stack
- Firsthand experience collecting and reviewing real-world malicious traffic
- A better understanding of how to extract actionable intelligence from honeypot logs to inform security decisions
- Step-by-step knowledge of deploying cloud infrastructure safely and affordably, even as a complete beginner

sessions.title: Intro to Secret Scanning Research
sessions.description:
Leaked secrets are everywhere, and scanning for them is relatively straightforward: download data, scan the data. Because of this, it's a rather saturated research area. Producing truly novel security research requires one of three things: new secret detection techniques, new secret detectors, or new sources for leaked secrets. 

In this 2-hour workshop, we'll walk attendees through the major OSS secret scanners: gitleaks, trufflehog, and kingfisher. We'll discuss the pros and cons of each, and when to use which. Then we'll show how to customize a brand new open-source tool, Betterleaks, a modern build of gitleaks. 

Live, during class, attendees will create detection signatures for never-before-detected secret types and then scan a few novel sources. 

Attendees will walk away having seen previously undetected secrets surfaced in real time, along with a repeatable process for producing novel research on their own.

This workshop is taught by two secret scanning experts:
- Zach Rice is the original author of Gitleaks and is actively building the next-generation secret scanner Betterleaks.
- Joe Leon formerly led secret scanning security research at Truffle Security, the company behind TruffleHog.

session.title: Breaking Hybrid Boundaries Across Azure and Windows
session.description:
Hybrid environments link on-premises systems with Azure cloud services, creating shared management and trust layers that organizations often assume secure by design. Our research shows how this assumption hides critical exposure across Microsoft hybrid components.
During assessments of Windows Admin Center and Azure Arc agent services, we uncovered five zero-day vulnerabilities that chain into full kill chains reaching from the local OS to the Azure tenant, including cross-tenant compromise.
The issues include a cryptographic flaw enabling unauthenticated cross-tenant influence, a local privilege escalation in WAC, token verification weaknesses allowing identity and authorization bypass, a chain of client and server-side validation flaws enabling RCE and AD compromise, and a race condition in Azure Arc that lets a low-privileged user hijack cloud identity and escalate to SYSTEM. These findings span two core Microsoft hybrid platforms and reveal how management services operating across host, cloud, and browser layers create pathways across boundaries normally isolated.
This presentation shows how attackers progress from unauthenticated external or low-privileged internal positions to full administrative control of both environments. Viewed through the lens of trust design, credential handling, and service initialization logic, the research exposes architectural blind spots common to hybrid platforms.
These findings earned $31,000 in bounty from Microsoft across five CVEs.

session.title: Finding Evil Fast: Windows Memory Triage with Volatility 3
session.description: Memory analysis is an essential investigative technique for detecting modern, memory-resident malware. Unfortunately, it is often perceived as a difficult and manual process requiring expert knowledge of operating systems and malware internals. This talk challenges that assumption by presenting five checks that can be automatically performed against Windows memory samples to quickly surface signs of malicious code execution or attacker access.  The presented checks answer five critical triage questions: 1) are any processes running with unexpected privileges, 2)  are restricted resources being accessed by unexpected processes, 3) are any processes executing code in a suspicious manner, 4) has malware entered the kernel, and 5) does any process or kernel driver match known threat intelligence? All checks will be demonstrated using Volatility 3, the most widely used open source framework for memory analysis. Attendees will leave with a compact workflow that SOC analysts, threat hunters, and incident handlers can use to automatically identify memory-only malware, toolkits, and attacker activity, helping them rapidly prioritize systems during large-scale triage and decide where deeper forensic analysis is warranted.

session.title: Rethinking CI/CD Security in the Age of GitHub Actions
session.description:
GitHub Actions can be scary. Growing exponentially, they have quietly become one of the most privileged execution environments in modern software delivery, and thus emerged as a major vector. They run on every commit, with access to secrets, cloud credentials, and deployment pipelines, yet many teams still treat them as harmless automations.

In several recent high-impact npm compromises, GitHub Actions were part of the attack surface as workflows were used to gain initial access and exfiltrate data. These incidents reveal a broader issue: Github actions are underestimated. These systems are deeply trusted, highly privileged, and often poorly secured.

This talk will break down common abuse patterns, explain why popular defensive advice falls short, and examine how third-party actions function as a largely unexamined dependency layer. You'll leave with practical ways to harden GitHub Actions, spot risky patterns, and keep your automation from becoming someone else's automation.

session.title: Feeling the heat from Malicious Packages? Cooloff with Cooldowns
session.description:
We’ve seen a surge in attacks that compromise third-party packages, resulting in costly and disruptive incident response for engineering and security teams.

The good news is that detection is getting faster. Many malicious package versions are identified and removed from public registries within hours or days of being published.

If you avoid installing recently released versions, you can dramatically reduce your exposure to these attacks. In response, package managers are introducing cooldowns—simple controls that delay adopting new releases long enough for malicious versions to be caught and removed.

In this talk, I'll share how we rolled out dependency cooldowns across multiple package managers at Semgrep. I’ll provide concrete examples and takeaways you can use to protect your organization without disrupting development workflows.

session.title: Authorization phishing: phishing, but without the creds
session.description:
Credential phishing used to be simple: trick a victim into typing their password into a fake login page, then reuse it. Then MFA meant a password alone wasn't enough. Attackers responded with real-time proxies to steal valid sessions via Attacker-in-the-Middle (AITM) phishing. Then we deployed passkeys, the "unphishable" factor, and attackers responded with MFA downgrade attacks against vulnerable backup methods.

But what if attackers could convince targets to grant account access without ever touching their credentials, where MFA and passkeys don't matter because the login isn't the target at all?

Authorization phishing is a growing class of attack abusing OAuth authorization flows rather than authentication. The umbrella includes consent phishing, device code phishing, and ConsentFix. 
These are being mass adopted as authentication controls mature and passkey adoption accelerates, giving attackers a technical and human advantage in unfamiliar phishing scenarios. Device code phishing has exploded from tiny volumes to a tier-1 threat in early 2026, while ConsentFix was newly discovered in late 2025 after a Russia-linked campaign.

This talk covers the history that led us here, technical details and demos of every attack, in-the-wild examples, and practical guidance on how organizations can prevent and detect them.

session.title: Every Repo, Every Org: OSS Package Triage on a Budget
session.description:
The last year has been a steady run of mass supply-chain compromises: Shai-Hulud x2, Trivy, axios, @antv... the list goes on. Some advisories have named as many as 600 affected packages which grows as the incident unfolds.

When one drops, your team needs to answer one question fast: are we affected, and where? For a small team that can't afford (or hasn't configured) SCA for every repository, that's a challenge. Your product repos might have SBOMs and CI, but your prototypes, internal tools, and the app Chad in Marketing vibe-coded probably don't.

To solve this ourselves, we built an open-source tool that helps us do three main things: 1) consolidate SBOMs for every repo across multiple GitHub orgs and ingest them into another excellent open source project called Dependency Track. 2) quickly parse a threat advisory's list of affected packages, and 3) query for all of them simultaneously to see if you're affected and where. 

The tool uses GitHub's free SBOM endpoint, so the only configuration cost is enabling one setting which we'll provide you a script to audit yourself. TCO for our usage is ~$100/month in AWS infrastructure charges.

In this talk, I'll walk through our previous and improved incident-response process, a live demo of the tool, and some additional automations our team has built now that we have consolidated coverage.  I'll also cover the limits of the approach, where we're still refining, and some things we learned along the way.

session.title: Beyond the Flag: How CTF Players Become Product Security Engineers
session.description:
Capture The Flag competitions are often dismissed as “just games,” but modern Product Security teams increasingly rely on the exact skills they develop: adversarial thinking, vulnerability analysis, exploit chaining, and secure design under pressure.

Whether you are an aspiring security professional or an experienced offensive security practitioner, in this session, you will learn a structured CTF-driven learning roadmap for developing practical security skills and will learn how hands-on, real-world customer-facing offensive engagements contribute to building deep product security expertise. We will also cover how AI capabilities are accelerating this journey of learning and securing the systems. Attendees will participate in a hands-on exercise to explore the challenge through the lenses of CTF problem solving, penetration testing, and Product Security.

session.title: Browser-Based Port Scanning in the Age of LNA
session.description:
Modern browsers are adding Local Network Access controls to prevent public websites from silently interacting with localhost and private-network services. But introducing a new security boundary also creates new browser behavior and new opportunities for unintended exposure.

This talk presents independent research into an unexpected side channel in the browser’s handling of local-network requests. From the context of a web page, it is possible to infer details about services reachable by a user’s browser without reading their responses or obtaining local-network permission.

Browser-based port scanning has historically been used for fingerprinting and tracking, helping websites infer which applications or services may be running on a device. Because the browser can reach both public and local network resources, this technique has important privacy and security implications.

I will explain how the behavior was discovered, how it was tested, and how it became a working proof of concept. The session will also cover the practical limits of the technique and what it reveals about security checks that occur before a permission decision is made.

session.title: 5.6 Million Domains, 400 GB of Code, Zero Alerts: How Nation-States Conduct Passive Intelligence
session.description: What if I told you that a solo researcher with open-source tools recovered 5.6 million government domains, 400+ gigabytes of source code, and 2.9 million developer identities across 73 countries, and triggered zero alerts? This talk reveals the methodology behind large-scale passive OSINT operations: how certificate logs, DNS enumeration, and git reconstruction expose government infrastructure at the nation-state level. Real findings include live credentials on election systems, military communications source code with valid authentication tokens, and supply chain vulnerabilities affecting critical infrastructure globally. For defenders: the clock is ticking, and you need to understand this threat model now.

session.title: Cleartext at the Edge: A Neptune R900 Case Study in RF Telemetry Exposure
session.description:
Security teams are trained to think in terms of networks, endpoints, cloud systems, identity, and applications. But many cyber-physical systems communicate through a layer that often sits outside traditional security visibility: radio frequency.
This talk presents a passive RF case study of Neptune R900 water meter telemetry and the broader security implications of cleartext AMR communications. Using low-cost software-defined radio tooling and receive-only observation, the research examines how wireless meter telemetry can expose structured data such as meter identifiers, consumption readings, status indicators, timestamps, and signal metadata before that data ever reaches utility-controlled systems.

The presentation walks through the RF security model, the AMR data flow from meter endpoint to utility systems, and the privacy risks created when repeated cleartext telemetry becomes pattern-of-life data. It also maps the findings to a qualitative risk model focused on likelihood, impact, and cyber-physical context. The discussion includes responsible research boundaries, disclosure considerations, and recommendations for utilities, vendors, and security teams.

Attendees will leave with a practical understanding of why RF telemetry should be treated as part of the attack surface, why legacy AMR design assumptions create modern privacy and trust-boundary risks, and how procurement, threat modeling, and architecture reviews can better account for signal-layer exposure.

session.title: Deep Link Vulnerabilities: When One Click Leads to Account Takeover
session.description:
Deep links are widely used in mobile applications to provide seamless navigation to specific screens inside an app. However, when deep links are improperly validated, they can become powerful attack vectors that allow external inputs to directly influence internal application behavior.

This lightning talk explores how seemingly harmless deep links can lead to serious security issues such as token leakage, WebView exploitation, and even one-click account takeover. 

In one example, a crafted deep link forces the app to open an attacker-controlled URL inside a WebView while automatically appending the victim’s authentication token, allowing the attacker to hijack the account with a single click.

We will also look at how vulnerable WebView configurations combined with exported deep link activities can enable attackers to exfiltrate session cookies, load malicious content, or execute privileged actions inside the app context.

This talk highlights common developer mistakes, demonstrates how attackers chain deep link handling with WebView behavior, and provides practical mitigation strategies to secure mobile applications against these hidden entry points.

session.title: It Costs More to Make Than It’s Worth: Lessons from the Penny for Your Sentinel Deployment
session.description:
The US penny was retired because it cost more to produce than its face value. A lot of Sentinel deployments have the same problem…data flowing into the wrong tier, connectors nobody is monitoring, and ingestion costs that don’t map to actual detection value. The difference is nobody retired the bad design.

This session connects three things most Sentinel engineers are treating as separate problems: ingestion visibility, tier architecture, and DCR design. We’ll use the new Data Insights Connector Observability preview as the diagnostic lens. A centralized dashboard that finally surfaces what’s flowing where, which connectors own which tables, and where ingestion anomalies are silently eroding your coverage is within reach.

From there we go deeper: how multi-destination DCRs let you deliberately split data streams at ingestion, routing high-fidelity events to Analytics for real-time detection while offloading lower-value telemetry to the data lake tier without losing it. And critically why that architectural decision only works if your observability is in place first.
